extracted.intended_audience: bibliometricians, scientometrics researchers, and research evaluators
extracted.subtask_description: A large-scale empirical analysis comparing Faculty of 1000 (F1000) post-publication recommendations with citation-based measures (citations, journal citation scores, and field-normalized citations) to assess the potential value of F1000 for research evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000 recommendation score (1/2/3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each recommendation has a score: 1 = 'good'; 2 = 'very good'; 3 = 'exceptional'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an expert quality judgment on individual publications; distribution observed in the data (58.6% score 1, 34.6% score 2, 6.9% score 3), with faculty being cautious in applying the 'exceptional' judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of recommendations per publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of how many times a publication has been recommended in F1000 (average 1.30 for recommended publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution is heavily skewed (81.1% of recommended publications have only one recommendation). The analysis treats both the maximum recommendation score and the (unweighted) total number of recommendations as relevant dimensions; observed diminishing marginal value of additional recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of recommendations (months from publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of months between a publication's appearance and when it receives an F1000 recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most recommendations are given shortly after (or sometimes before) publication: over 80% are between the second month before and the fourth month after appearance; fewer than 10% are given six or more months after; interpretation should be cautious because official publication month may differ from when the work became publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation coverage/selectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of publications in the biomedical literature that receive at least one F1000 recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 2% of biomedical publications receive at least one recommendation (exact percentage depends on literature delineation); this low coverage is central to interpreting the relationship with citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation activity by field (WoS subject categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of publications with one or more recommendations per Web of Science journal subject category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation activity is very uneven across fields (e.g., Multidisciplinary sciences 11.8%, cell biology and developmental biology high; surgery low ~0.5%). Fractional counting is used when publications belong to multiple subject categories. Uneven distribution affects comparisons and field-normalized analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching F1000 records to Web of Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to link an F1000 recommended publication to a WoS record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A link is established if either the DOI is the same or journal title, volume number, issue number, and first author name (last name and initials) match perfectly. The matching procedure is conservative to minimize incorrect matches; manual cleaning of common journal titles was performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of special recommendations (F1000 Reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some recommendations originate from review articles in F1000 Reports Biology and Medicine and are included in the same way as ordinary recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the data set these special recommendations cannot be distinguished from ordinary ones and were included; F1000 suggested these may tend to be given to older publications, but this was not verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of non-recommendation dissent records
rubrics_metrics.description: Records in the F1000 data that do not have a recommendation score (dissenting opinions) are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 182 such records (indicating disagreement with another faculty member's recommendation) were removed from analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation counting window (three-year window)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations are counted in the year of publication and the next two years (three-year citation window).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations were also restricted to those given in the publication year or within the next two years to ensure fair comparability between recommendations and citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal Citation Score (JCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a publication in journal X, JCS equals the average number of citations received by all publications in journal X in 2006–2009 (articles and reviews), counted within a three-year window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JCS is used as a comparator/predictor for publication-level citations; average JCS in the analyzed set was 7.3. JCS often correlates more strongly with publication citations than recommendations do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microfield classification and field-normalized citation score
rubrics_metrics.description: Each publication is assigned to a 'microfield' in a publication-level classification system; field-normalized citation score = publication citations divided by average citations of all publications in the same microfield (2006–2009).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microfield system contains 22,412 microfields (each 50 to a few thousand publications). Field-normalization is used to account for differences in citation behavior across fields and to identify top 1% highly cited publications per microfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pearson correlation to assess association
rubrics_metrics.description: Pearson correlation coefficients are calculated between recommendation measures (maximum score, number, weighted number) and citation measures (number of citations, JCS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported correlations: e.g., max recommendation score vs citations ~0.24, vs JCS ~0.33; number/weighted number of recommendations slightly higher. JCS-citations correlation reported ~0.52, indicating JCS predicts citations better than recommendations by Pearson correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting recommendations via least-squares regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine weights for 'good', 'very good', 'exceptional' recommendations by regressing citations (or JCS) on counts of each recommendation type to maximize correlation/predictive fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regression-derived relative weights (from number-of-citations regression) suggest a 'very good' recommendation should be ~1.8 times a 'good', and 'exceptional' ~2.5 times a 'good'. These weights are similar to F1000's 1/2/3 scheme; weighting marginally increases correlations because most publications have no recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision–recall analysis for identifying top 1% highly cited publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision and recall are computed for approaches (based on JCS, maximum recommendation score, unweighted number of recommendations, weighted number) to identify the top 1% most highly cited publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JCS-based approach outperforms recommendation-based approaches; only ~26.3% of top 1% highly cited publications had at least one recommendation in the global (non-field-normalized) analysis, demonstrating limited recall of recommendations for highly cited items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-normalized precision–recall (top 1% per microfield)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify top 1% highly cited publications per microfield and evaluate approaches (field-normalized JCS, recommendations) by precision–recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field normalization worsened performance (precision) for all approaches; only 20.1% of top 1% per-microfield publications had been recommended at least once, suggesting recommendation activity correlates with fields of high citation density and uneven coverage affects normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrap for confidence intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: 95% confidence intervals reported for means, regression coefficients, and correlations were obtained using bootstrapping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bootstrapping (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993) provides empirical CIs for summary statistics throughout the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity test excluding very high-impact journals
rubrics_metrics.description: A robustness check excluded publications in journals with JCS above 50 (e.g., Nature, Science, Cell, NEJM) to see influence of high-impact journals on results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding these publications (about 0.9% of the 1.7M) produced substantially worse precision/recall results for both JCS and recommendations, indicating high-impact journals contribute importantly to identification performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractional counting for multi-category journal subject assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: When publications belong to multiple WoS subject categories, counts are fractionalized across categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fractional counting was applied to calculate the proportion of publications with recommendations per subject category to avoid double-counting and to fairly allocate multi-category publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive cautions and possible biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential explanations and caveats for differences between recommendations and citations include: recommendations may capture a different 'type' of impact (expert quality) versus citations (author impact), uneven distribution of faculty across fields, cronyism, and geographic bias in F1000's faculty nomination system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that low coverage (≈98% of publications not recommended) and uneven field representation limit the extent to which recommendations can substitute for citation-based measures; resolving whether recommendations identify different valuable outputs requires further qualitative investigation of faculty reasons and nomination system biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative matching trade-off guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A conservative matching procedure (requiring perfect matches on bibliographic fields or DOI) reduces incorrect matches at the cost of leaving some matches unmatched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors chose conservatism to expect almost no incorrect matches; note that a less conservative approach would produce more matches but likely more errors—an explicit methodological choice affecting downstream statistics (matching rate reported 93.2%).
